utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Ekkehard Withopf with the case manager, Kimberly Fleming. And we are joined today by Mrs. Charlotte Verhaeghe, who is an intern within the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic. Stephane Bourgon is co-counsel. And Mirna Milanovic is the legal assistant. We represent General Hadzihasanovic. In accordance with the decision of the Court, General Hadzihasanovic is not present. He has been temporarily released to attend his brother's funeral. We would like to take this opportunity to thank the Trial Chamber for having taken such a decision. And in accordance with the Trial Chamber's decision, General Hadzihasanovic will be returning tomorrow to The Hague, and he will attend the hearing on Wednesday. Thank you. And similarly, General Hadzihasanovic has agreed to us attending the hearing and to the hearing being conducted without his presence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could Mr. Kubura's Defence introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Mulalic, represent Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused, Mr. Kubura. As everyone has noticed, one of the accused is not present today, since a member of his family has died, and his Defence requested over the weekend to be granted leave to attend his brother's funeral. The authorities of his country have taken charge of him, and he will be back in The Hague tomorrow and will attend the hearing on Wednesday, naturally. In accordance with the request -- in the request, the Defence said that they would represent the accused, and this was with the accused's agreement. So the hearing can be held without the accused being present but with the presence of his Defence team. Today there are two witnesses who have been scheduled. And before calling the witnesses in, could the Prosecution inform us of the time they think they will need to examine both witnesses. Mr. Withopf or Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, we anticipate that we can complete the examination of both witnesses today. We anticipate for the first witness examination-in-chief of about some 45 minutes; the second witness, we anticipate examination-in-chief of about some 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the usher please call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Niko Petrovic. I'm from Kakanj. I was born on the 19th of April, 1965, in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a central-heating fitter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where do you live? In which city do you live at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will now make a solemn declaration, and the usher will show you the text. Could you please read it out. Aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're going to anxious the questions that will be put to you by the representative or the representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right. We have been informed that the examination will last for about 45 minutes. After they have put their questions to you, the Defence, which is to your left, will cross-examine you. And if the need arises, the Judges, who are sitting before you, will also ask you some questions. Please answer as extensively as possible the questions put to you. And if you don't understand the questions, ask the person who is putting the question to you to rephrase it or ask the question again. Try to avoid yes-or-no answers and to provide answers that are as complete as possible. Having said that, the Prosecution may proceed with its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, where were you living in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber the state of ethnic relations between the different groups in Kakanj in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The inter-ethnic relations in Kakanj in 1992 were somewhat tense because there'd been a splitting of Bosnia, a separation, a division. Through the media they'd started dividing into three republics. One was to be Serbia; one was to be Bosnia and Herzegovina; one was to belong to the Croats -- one part was to belong to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992 how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I worked in the Velepromet Visoko labour organisation in Kakanj. It was a labour organisation, a company in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of work were you employed doing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, the shop started closing down. And then I worked as a driver. I was helping a driver. Since there was a driver in the labour organisation, I helped him. And I would receive orders from that organisation. The shops were closing down at the time, since there was a financial crisis during that period. So we'd drive this stock around, as the shops closed down. And after a few days, after some days had passed - this was just before bankruptcy - it was no longer possible there were no funds any more. The employers -- the employees weren't receiving their salaries. That was just before the conflict broke out. So I worked as a driver. I transported this stock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you just mentioned the conflict breaking out. Do you recall when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, these conflicts -- it was around 1992 when they broke out. Some kind of a group entered and was captured somewhere in the Croatian area, towards Kraljeva Sutjeska some kind of Mujahedin appeared, so the HVO captured some of those Mujahedin and then the civilians, who were given some kind of a work obligation - but we were totally innocent, since we weren't members of any formation; we were just Croats or Orthodox -- of the Orthodox faith - they started bringing us in. So if something happened to one of theirs, then something would happen to us. The situation was tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when did the armed conflict begin in Kakanj, where you were living?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conflict in Kakanj broke out after 1993, after I had been wounded. On the 18th of May, 1993, I had an accident. After that, I stayed on in Kakanj for four days, and then I took the risk and went with my grandmother and my wife. I went to Kiseljak. At the time, this was very risky because there weren't any cars on the road at the time or anything similar. People were hiding at the time. No one appeared there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a slight correction to the translation. Line 13, the translation states "after I was wounded." The witness said "after he had a misfortune, an accident."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was brought in on the 18th of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just a matter of the translator having misheard something. Instead of "accident," it says "wounded here." Instead of "misfortune," it says "wounded." So I would be grateful if this error could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You've heard what the Defence has said. The Defence believes that you said "the accident I had," whereas the English text we have in front of us says "after I was wounded." So what is the correct term, "wounded" or "had an accident"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an accident in 1993. I was brought in to the motel by the MOS, the Muslim armed forces, a civilian victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you weren't physically wounded. You didn't have any wounds, any physical wounds, any wounds to your body. Or perhaps you had psychological wounds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had wounds after I was questioned in the motel. That's the occasion on which they brought 15 of us in, in total. And after that, a baton was used and my head was cracked. I was covered in blood. I had stitches to my head. You can see this in the medical documentation. I was dealt blows to the head. Yes, I had open wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution may continue with its examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've mentioned 18 May 1993. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you had at that time any military obligation; that is, were you a soldier in any military unit or organisation on 18 May 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. On the 18th of May, 1993, I was at home in the morning. And before, in the organisation where I worked, this was a sort of Territorial Defence staff and they were assigned duties. And on that fateful day, on the 18th, in the morning I was at home. I was free. And sometime in the afternoon that group appeared. They had some sort of signs around their heads, green bands. I wasn't a member of any formation. I had Territorial Defence duties, and I had work obligations to fulfil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please explain for us what you mean when you said "I had Territorial Defence duties." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence, for all those employees, it appeared as if each company had to find guards. And when we weren't working, then there were certain facilities that we had to guard and the things that were part of the organisation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, what things or places were you required to guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: They asked me - and not just myself but other employees too - to guard the main office. That's where the documents were. So yes, the main office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The main office, Witness, of what organisation or company?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The main office of the Sretno Kakanj organisation, the Velepromet organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what kind of organisation was Sretno Kakanj, the Velepromet organisation? What was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this main office, this is where they had all the revenue from the sales, from the trade, because Velepromet was involved in mixed goods. They sold mixed goods, household appliances, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So Velepromet was a company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you wear when you served as a guard at this company?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, but we were issued a pistol. It was what the porters would have. And this pistol would be handed over to each person whenever he turned up for duty, whenever a person took over those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us a few moments ago that on 18 May 1993 a group appeared. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber approximately what time you saw this group and where you were when you saw them.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: That group of people appeared about 100 metres from my house on the lower side of the Bosna River and from the Sretno Motel in Kakanj it was about 150 to 200 metres away. They appeared from below. There were ten of them in the group. At the time, I was in front of my house. I saw how the neighbours were there in front of my house, and they were escorting them one by one. They were bringing them all in with their identity cards, all those who weren't Muslims. They would only bring in those of the Orthodox and Catholic faiths, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this group come to your house, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that group did come to my house. My father, being a civilised man, asked them what they needed and what they were after. They said, "We're only surveying the area here." He called them in, offered them coffee. It was May; it was warm outside. My mother made them some coffee, which they had outside. And then my father sent me to get water from the source, since the source is about 20 metres -- the spring is about 20 metres from my house. I took a container and went to get water. Five of them got up, and they said, "You too can give us your identity card," and they took me away too with my identity card. I don't know what happened then. But they took me away in my slippers allegedly to give some sort of statement with regard to the Sretno Motel in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, approximately what time of day was it on 18 May 1993 when they took you away?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about 12.00 or half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They took me to the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, how far was it approximately from your house to Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The motel was about 150 to 200 metres from my house. I can see the motel from my house even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get from your house to the motel?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: It took me about five minutes to get to the motel from my house, since two men went with me. I was walking in front of them. I was taken there via a shortcut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The two men who took you to Motel Sretno, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: These two men had a wide green band around their heads and around the left arm. They also had a green band but it was narrower, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were they carrying any type of arms?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were carrying automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened immediately upon your arrival at Motel Sretno on 18 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you exactly what happened. When I got to the motel, well, the experience I went through was incredible. I didn't believe that it was possible for people to act as if they weren't men. I don't know how else to put it. When they gathered all of us there - there were about 15 of us, as I said, perhaps -- well, give or take a man - but at the time I don't think the number is important. What is important is how people can mistreat others without any pangs of conscience. First we entered that basement in the Sretno Motel. There was a fairly wide room at the entrance and there was another one, which was narrower, which they threw us into. Once they had done that, there was one chair in the wider area, and then three of them said, "come out to this chair one by one," so they could obtain information. And so I could see what would happen, I was the first who stood up. I was a little large and I thought I was more resistant, tougher than the others. I wanted to see what they wanted. However, the worst things happened to me. I sat down on the chair. One stood to the left. He was armed. Another person stood to the right. And there was one who was facing me; he was in front of me. I was sitting in the same position I'm sitting in now. He asked me what my name was, and I told him, "My name is Niko Petrovic." He said, "No, you're not." I told him again, "I'm Niko Petrovic." He started rubbing my fingers with -- my toes with his boot. He said, "Now we'll see. You're an Ustasha. Let's see how bad your Ustasha blood smells." All of a sudden he shouted out, "What are you waiting for? Why aren't you hitting him?" And as this person said so, the person to the right, he hit me with his military-issue boot in the temple. This can all be seen in the medical documentation. So he kicked me in the temple, and he injured me here. When I was kicked, naturally I moved to the left. But on the other side, the other person was waiting for me there and he hit me with the rifle butt. So I was returned to the original position. And then the person who was in front of me, who said that my blood smelt and said it wasn't my fault if I was Niko Petrovic, he kicked me in the chest and I reeled back and then the next person shouted out. They pushed me back to where the people were detained, and then they proceeded in this fashion one by one. Can I continue like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just stop you for one moment. When you say "they proceeded in this fashion one by one," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've just said "they pushed me back to where the people were detained, and then they proceeded in this fashion one by one." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean that as there were three of them there, they returned me inside and another person was taken out and they said, "Next." So he, that person, was to go through the same thing that I'd been through. Nothing else. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the chair that you were taken to, where was that chair in relation to the room where you and the others were detained?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The chair was in the middle of that larger part of the room, which is where you could see the others, which is where they could look to see what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you were sitting in the chair being interrogated and mistreated, could you see the other detainees in the room behind the bars?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that there was approximately 15 individuals detained in the room with you. Do you recall the names of any of those other individuals?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can remember the names. Ljubisa Vucenovic, Josip Marusic; Zeljko Krkeljas, Mladenko Krkeljas, two brothers who had to hit each other. After we'd been taken out the second time, we were forced to see brothers hitting each other and mistreating each other in accordance with others' orders, who observed that. They had to do this in this bloody manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you about that in just a moment. First let me ask you a couple more questions about the interrogation. Do you know how many of the other men that were detained with you were similarly interrogated and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many other people -- or rather, what do you mean "others"? There were 15 of us there, and we were all mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once you were returned to the room, did you personally see the others being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all mistreated. All 15 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you saw happening to the other men that had been detained with you in that room.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you exactly. They didn't fare any better than I did. In that first round, as there were -- people were taken out several times. This was the first round of it. But the same thing happened. So it was a sort of warning to us to tell us what we could expect in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago, Witness, that you saw brothers hitting each other. Can you tell us when this happened and the circumstances surrounding that, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. I can tell you the circumstances too. Some half an hour went by from that first beating and the provocations and the way they took it out on me. They came back in larger numbers. A group of about ten of them came in. They were armed. We didn't have anything, of course, and we weren't to blame for anything. And they lined us up. They took us out of the small room we were in and took us out to this larger space and made us face each other. And then they forced us, as we were facing one another, to slap one another so that brother would slap brother. I slapped the person standing next to me -- or, rather, my neighbour. And it's difficult to have to do that. I lifted my hand and was going to slap him, but I just didn't have the heart. I just couldn't do it. So my hand stopped in midair. And then the HOS man -- or MOS man insulted me and called me an Ustasha and why didn't I hit him. And then I was hit on the back with a rifle butt. And that's what happened to anybody who refused to do what they told them, so that you would see brothers slapping each other and neighbours slapping each other. And after that they told us to hit each other in the stomach as hard as we could. And I still have haematoma as a result of that and I have medical papers to prove it. And not only me, but others too. And I considered that one of those 15 of us who were beaten succumbed to the wounds and one of them -- one of us died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the people who were detaining you, what were they wearing? What type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't call them "people." They weren't civilised. But all right, let's say "people." They were wearing camouflage uniforms. And when night fell, they would mask themselves, and that was part three of the way in which they took it out on us, if I can put it that way. I said at the beginning that they had green bands tied round their heads and this insignia or this marking round their arms, and the BH Army had its separate signs too, markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what unit or organisation did these people that were detaining you belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: These people belonged to -- they were members of a unit. They belonged to the Muslim armed forces, the MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you just mentioned the third part, as you put it, or in the English translation it was described as "the third part." Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what the third part of the mistreatment that you received on 18 May 1993 was comprised of.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe that for you. The third part or part three was the most terrible part, as far as I was concerned. They lined up along the corridor, going out of the small room into the larger hall. Some of them were on the left-hand side of the wall; the others were on the right-hand side. And one of them - and we know who issued the orders - said, "Who's Mijo's son? Let him step out of line himself. It would be better for him to come forward himself, rather than wait for us to take him out." He was beaten numb. I stepped out. As soon as I had taken a step forward, I didn't have to take any more steps. I was beaten with a rifle butt on my back, and then I was kicked by one of them, then another, and a third. And I did what I could to protect myself with my arms. I raised my arms to my head. But they weren't able to get me down to the ground. Then I tried to cross over to my colleagues, to be with, as close to them as possible, but they got me with their rifle butts. And they used great force, and I fell to the ground by that small room, by the door. When I fell to the ground, I began to lose consciousness, and one of them kneeled down on my back and took a baton. And the other witnesses can testify to that, the people who were with me there. They counted. And he hit me 14 times with this baton on my head. There was blood spurting out all over the place, from one wall to the other. He cocked his rifle at, me, his pistol at me. And he said, "I'm going to kill this Ustasha now." Although -- I'll never come to terms with that fact. I have my own name and surname. I'll never agree to that. And just as I was about to lose consciousness, I heard a voice which seemed to come from afar. He was a school friend of mine, actually. I don't know how he happened to be in that group, in that MOS group. Allegedly he heard from somebody else that I was there or something like that, but anyway I heard his voice. I suddenly heard a familiar voice, and it was the voice of my school friend, whose name was Asim Music. And I can consider that that man ought to be protected and taken care of because he and a colleague of his pushed me inside and from that same MOS group they were beaten themselves. They were beaten up very badly for locking the room up and preventing anybody else from going inside. He said, "I'm not going to leave here until you are released, until they release you." So I think that there were always people with good human feelings, and I think that that man ought to be supported, along with his friend, his colleague. And there were parts of his own body that were thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, following the intervention of Asim Music, were you mistreated on any other occasion on 18 May 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Asim took the key to the lock away and several others turned up and they started shouting. We had to call out "Allah-U-Ekber" and things like that. We were forced to do that. And whenever they said this to us, we would have to respond in similar fashion. But I didn't actually utter those words of greeting. Everybody should protect themselves. But anyway, he locked us in and then left. Then a couple of others arrived. They didn't know what to do. They took a piece of wood and told us to rest our heads on the bars, iron bars, and that we should stand one behind another and that they would give us something for a good night -- they'd give us a good-night beating. And that was the last time they beat us that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, as a result of the beatings that you received on 18 May 1993, the cumulative results of those various beatings, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the injuries that you sustained.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: During the three beatings, I had open fractures -- open wounds to my skull, 5 centimetres I think one was. But my head was all beaten up and cut, cut open. I had bruises and haematoma by my kidneys and the zygomatic bone, and you can see all this in the medical report. My back was all black and blue, haematomas all over in the region of my abdomen, and they were the size of a fist. That was what the doctor said. But he wasn't able to transfer me to one of the larger medical centres, to a hospital, so that I was dragged to Haljinici where first aid was administered. I was given an intravenous drip, first of all. And after I had recovered, I took my wife and my grandmother and left Kakanj and went to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when were you released from the basement detention facility of the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: They released us on the 19th, which was the next day. They released us on the 19th. A representative of the BH Army arrived. He introduced himself and said that he was a representative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and he collected us up there. We all had to give our particulars to tell them where -- which relatives they had, brothers, sisters, et cetera. So he took down our particulars. And with this certificate, saying that what had happened to us was not done by the army but that it was done by the MOS, the Muslim armed forces, and that we must fight together. That's what the man said. And he said he was from Visoko and that we all had to fight against the one aggressor in the area, which was the Serbs. They released us at about 12.20 -- or rather, between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at the time the representative of the BH Army arrived, were the wounds that you had sustained visible or had you already been medically treated at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The wounds were visible, but they would say, "Ah, did anybody beat you?" I didn't actually have a mirror to see for myself what I looked like. What I want to say is that nobody administered first aid, nor could they do so. Who's going to give you first aid in the basement of a motel? It wasn't a hotel, it was just a motel. Allegedly they said that your car would drive you home, but I said, "I'll go to my own house on foot," and I crossed the railway track. I didn't know what happened to me, but on the way to my house, which was 150 to 200 metres away, I could see that the women were looking away from me. They were putting their hands up to their eyes and they didn't know what had happened to me, but they didn't want to see what I -- the way I looked. When I arrived home -- well, it was all very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, shortly after you arrived home, you sought the medical treatment that you've described for us a few moments ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived home, and my father went to have a good cry. He wasn't able to look at me. My mother, as any mother would, swore, but she said, "Everything will be all right." She took me -- brought me some water. I washed my hair with it. I didn't realise that my head was all cut up. I put some shampoo on it and started washing it with the water, but my head started bleeding and I told my wife to bring a towel and to put it round me. Marinko Marusic arrived at that moment, with his brother Josip Marusic. We got into my own car - I was in that state - and I went straight to the medical centre. I was received there. And I'd like to say thank you to them all there. Five doctors - not one - five doctors came to help me, to give medical treatment. They didn't mind who I was. Then I went back home. And when I got there, there was somebody waiting for me by the garage. There was the French Battalion in Kakanj there, and they had an interpreter, and the man had come to see what had happened to me. He said he would protect us. I just showed him the top half of my body, and I said, "There's no protection that you can give me. My health was left completely unprotected and this is the state I'm in."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the Judges has a question to ask you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you two questions. The first is this: The people who were detained with you and who were mistreated, like you, were they all civilians or were some of them soldiers? And my second question is this: Were there any women detainees with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: As to your first question, they were all civilians. And your second question: There were no women; just men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We still have about 20 minutes before the break, so I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Petrovic. My name is Edina Residovic. I am the Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I'm going to ask you a few questions. You said that you were born in Kakanj and that that is where you lived, up until 1993, and that you also live in Kakanj today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my colleague, you also said that from 1992 you worked as a driver in the Velepromet firm of Visoko, their branch office in Kakanj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Petrovic: During that period of time - that is to say, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 - in going about your duties as a driver, did you tour the broader area around Kakanj towards Visoko, Kiseljak, Busovaca, Zenica? Did you drive that way?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did go as far as Visoko, because that's where Velepromet had an office. Perhaps I'd go there once a week, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before these events came to pass, what happened to you on the 18th of May, is it true that in Kakanj there were no conflicts between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no conflicts. No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, because of the conflict that was going on not far from you, there was a certain amount of tension among the population in Kakanj. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In going about your duties as a driver and also through the information media, you were informed that an armed conflict had taken place between the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and the Croatian Defence Council in the broader area of Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you said that when you went about your job as a driver, you went to Visoko and other places. Now, I'm interested in knowing the following: While you were going about your duties, did you learn that at the beginning of 1993 in the surrounding places, towns -- Busovaca, Kiseljak, Vitez, and so on -- that there were open armed conflict which had taken place between the BH Army and the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that did not happen. That happened after the 18th of May, which is when the conflicts broke out, a month later, between the HVO and the BH Army. But at that time, there were no conflicts, while I was driving, while I was a driver and drove along those roads. But yes, there were tensions. There was increased tension; that's true. And you would see slogans written up saying this territory belongs to so and so, this territory belongs to the other side, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993, you said that you did not belong to any military formation but that you were doing your work assignment in the company you worked for; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: After that, and up to the end of the war, did you join a military formation of any kind at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I joined a military formation in 1993, after Fojnica fell. And I have medical documents to bear this out. I went for a medical examination, and I was to report again to the doctor ten days later, to go to the military hospital for a checkup. However, I was not able to do so because the army had assumed control of Fojnica, so that that upper part of Fojnica, in the direction of Dusina, that was, and then they forced me to join up. The diagnosis that I was given was that I should rest, but they and the HVO forced me to take up arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So from mid-1993 until the end of the war, you were in fact a member of the HVO; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council was in Grude, is that right, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was in Fojnica myself, and it belonged to Kiseljak, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you said that there was some tension in Kakanj too. Is it true that in Kakanj at that time an HVO brigade existed whose headquarters used to be in the centre of town but as of April 1993 it was relocated to the village of Haljinici, which was 5 kilometres east of Kakanj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of April and the beginning of May, you were able to notice that some of the Croatian inhabitants from Kakanj were withdrawing towards Vares and Busovaca. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I left Kakanj after my misfortunes, four days later, that is, so I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that at the beginning of 1993 quite a lot of refugees from the area of Busovaca, Kiseljak, Vitez started arriving in Kakanj? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. The refugees were arriving from Ilijas, for the most part, during that period that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When they took you to the Sretno Motel, would it be true to say that in the course of this terrible experience you went through the persons who maltreated you had painted faces? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just repeat what you said. Your school companion appeared from somewhere, and he in fact helped you on that occasion and prevented them from mistreating you or carrying on to mistreat you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the army representatives arrived, after a short discussion with you, you were released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you said, in the local hospital in Kakanj you were provided with urgent medical treatment and the document states that you had an open wound which was 5 centimetres long and extended as far as the bone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at the time, you didn't have a fractured skull; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that wound was stitched up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, when you were examined in the hospital in Kakanj, you were taken to Haljinici, to the HVO hospital, and you were provided with other forms of treatment, other medicine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, an HVO ambulance took you with your family to Fojnica, and for a certain period of time you continued to receive treatment in the HVO military hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. My wife, my grandmother, and myself went there in my own car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From 1997 you have had certain problems and you've been receiving treatment from a neuropsychiatrist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Mr. Kubura's Defence have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We just have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you confirm for the Trial Chamber that, as you have said in your testimony today, you stayed in the Sretno Motel for no more than 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, when you left the Sretno Motel, you said, in response to my colleague's question, you said you went to the clinic, where you were provided with medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the medical treatment was of a high standard and that there were five doctors who took care of you.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You weren't detained for treatment in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't detained for treatment in the clinic, because the doctor wasn't able to transfer me to another clinical centre, a high clinical centre for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The letter of discharge was signed by Dr. Spasojevic after your examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence suggest that is this exhibit -- the letter of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discharge be shown to the witness, so he can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence team received this document from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the letter of discharge that you received on that day, when you'd been provided with the medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is just the first document that has to do with my checkup by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The day after you'd left the Sretno Motel?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the day after I'd left the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In this document that you have been shown, the Dr. Spasojevic stated that you had only minor wounds.

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the document states that the patient -- that he wasn't in a position to send the patient to another medical centre for further and more detailed examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we suggest that this document be tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit, because the witness stated that he had a fracture of the skull, whereas the medical documentation states something that is quite contrary to his statement. We will ensure that a sufficient number of copies are provided of this document in the Bosnian -- in B/C/S and in English. We have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you will put your first and last name on this document. You will sign the document, please, and make a note of the date. Please make a note of your first and last name and of the date. It's the 19th of January, 2004, today. So we have the document in B/C/S and an English translation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution has something? It's a document that was provided by the Prosecution. Any comments on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections. Could you show this document to Mr. Kubura. Very well. The Defence, they should have a look. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number but for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S version will have the exhibit number DK3; the English version will have the exhibit number DK3E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution takes the floor to ask further questions, Witness, the Judges who are before you have been carefully following the questions put to you both by the Prosecution and the Defence. It seems, on the basis of what you said in response to a question from the Defence, that from 1997 you have had neurological problems. In your opinion, the problems that you have had since 1997, are they related to what happened in the Sretno Motel?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The medical documents from 1993 establish a connection. Before, I didn't have any ailments of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have heard the question put to you by the Defence. The Defence said that when the doctors examined you, according to the document, they stated that your wounds were slight. But you say that there is an additional examination. Is that correct? That there should have been an additional examination which didn't take place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO PETROVIC
utterances.text: That was a local clinic, and that's why there was no such additional examination. And I would like to repeat that the doctor couldn't send me anywhere else from Kakanj, because that was the situation. He couldn't send me to another clinic for further and more detailed examinations. But the finding also contains other findings that are related, and all this happened on that fateful day, on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution have any other further questions, having heard the questions put to the witness by the Defence? If so, I will ask you to be rapid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your examination has been concluded since the Prosecution has used up the time that they had scheduled for you. And the Defence has also examined you. You have answered their questions. And you have answered the Judges' questions too. We would like to thank you for having come to The Hague, and we wish you a good trip home. I'm now going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter to 4.00. We will now adjourn for 25 minutes, and the hear willing resume -- the hearing will resume at ten past 4.00 for the examination of the second witness who has been scheduled for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will call the next witness into the courtroom, and we will continue with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Marinko Marusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of June, 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a forestry engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what do you do at the moment? What is your job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm involved in some kind of private business in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now live in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The usher, who is standing by you, will show you a text. It's the solemn declaration that you have to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just taken the solemn declaration. You will now have to answer the Prosecution's questions. They are to your right. They will be examining for about an hour and 45 minutes. After they have examined you, the Defence, to your left, will also ask you some questions. And if necessary, the Judges who are sitting before you will also ask you some questions. You should attempt to answer the questions as precisely as possible. Avoid answering yes or no to answers. You should elaborate on your answers. And if there is a question that you don't understand, ask the person asking you to question to repeat it. The Prosecution may now take the floor to proceed with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to whether you have been -- as to whether you have served in any army.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I haven't served in any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us in respect to the reason why not.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I haven't served in an army because as a child I wounded my -- I injured my left eye, so my vision in my left eye has been affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In May 1993, Mr. Marusic, where did you live in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was living in Kakanj in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us since when in May 1993 you lived in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was working in Travnik. I worked in Travnik until 1992. But when the war broke out in Bosnia, I went to Kakanj in 1992, perhaps in June or July, because the flat that I had in Travnik, I gave it to Dautovic Smail, a friend of mine, I thought he could live in it. And I went to Kakanj because I thought it was a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there an earlier point in time when you used to live in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1964 I moved to Kakanj. I spent my entire childhood there. I completed primary school there and then secondary school. After that, I studied in Sarajevo. But I would also go to Kakanj. So, in fact, I lived in Kakanj right up until 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the people living in Kakanj at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, the people living in Kakanj, well, they were members of various ethnic -- of all the ethnic groups. The majority were Bosniaks, and Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How would you describe the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats in early 1993 in the region of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the relations between those two peoples were good, one could say. But the policies conducted were such that they were attempting to make the relations between those two peoples deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did there come a point in time in 1993 when the relations actually deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The relations deteriorated for good on the 18th of May, 1993. That is when the conflict between -- well, we can put it this way, between the Croats and the Muslims actually broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 18th of May, 1993, what did you do on the 18th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1993, I was in my parents' house, naturally. I was outside. I was with my son. He was only three years old. He was born in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time on the 18th of May, 1993 when you have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of May, 1993, some units entered our settlement. They were in uniform. And they knew exactly which houses were inhabited by Croats or Serbs, and they'd go up to those houses and they started assembling us. And they picked me up in the street too in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you provide us, please, some more details about the units which have entered your settlement.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. These units were based in the motel, which was more or less an integral part of our local commune, as we called it. We called those units the Muslim armed forces, or MOS would be the abbreviated form. They were in uniform. They had green headbands on them, and they also had green bands on their arms, and on some of them these bands bore the inscription "The police."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning, Mr. Marusic, that these units were based in the motel. Can you please tell us which motel you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a motel which is at the railway station or, rather, close to the railway station in Kakanj. It's naturally black. That's our symbol in Kakanj. It's in the shape of a piece of coal, because Kakanj is a mining village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is there a name, Mr. Marusic, which is used to describe this motel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: The name of the motel? Well, we called it "the motel." At the moment, it's called a hotel. That's what it says on the building now. Whether it's a matter of categories, I don't know. But I know that when it was built and when it opened for business, I know that it was called a motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P10. I understand that the ELMO is not working. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the photograph please be put on the ELMO. Is my conclusion correct that it is not working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, apparently it's not working. So we should use the photograph, then, unless you have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: My intention was to use Sanction, Mr. President, but I have been informed that Sanction isn't working either today. So I would like to have the photograph be put in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, can you explain what you can see on the photograph that has been put in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: On the photograph, I can see the motel. That's the building we were incarcerated in and beaten up. And in front of the motel - I don't know whether you can see it - but I can see a parking lot, and my house is situated behind the motel, about 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to the units which arrested you. To your knowledge, were these units based in this hotel -- in this motel you can see on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Those units were in this facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were describing the individuals which arrested you as wearing uniforms. Did you recognise any military insignia on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were wearing uniforms specific to those units. Mostly they had green bands around their heads and around their arms, bands or ribbons. And on their belts they had two crossed sabres or knives, and it said "Muslim armed forces" on it. And we abbreviated that to MOS, which is what we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall as to whether there was something else on this emblem?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember - and that was 11 years ago now - they were like two crossed sabres. That was the insignia. And I think that the outlines of a territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were embossed on it too, and that it said "Muslim armed forces," and I think that territory was also covered in green. It was green.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you were arrested on the 18th of May, 1993, have you been told anything at the time you have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. When I was arrested, they didn't say anything, but they knew full well who they were supposed to arrest. They didn't let us talk to each other. I was wearing women's slippers, actually, at the time, because I was looking after my son and I happened to have them on. The gentleman who -- rather, the man who arrested me didn't allow me to go back into my house to take my personal documents with me, nor did he let me change into some shoes or some proper slippers. But he just cocked an automatic rifle at me and ordered me to march ahead in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Where did the soldier order you to march to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: He had his rifle pointed at me, and he ordered me to start walking towards the motel. We didn't take the route that is usually taken. He led me across the courtyards of other houses, took a shortcut. So I had to jump across fences and walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are talking about the 18th of May, 1993. At what point in time during the day was it when you were ordered to walk to the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in the afternoon, around 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get to know prior to arriving at the Motel Sretno as to whether other people have been arrested as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know. They told us that some units were going around arresting Serbs and Croats at random. And before they arrested me, they'd already taken away my brother and a friend of mine, Ljubisa Vucenovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the full name of your brother.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Josip Marusic. And he was born in 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the Motel Sretno, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: May I just be allowed to add one more point? While they were taking me through my village, there were some neighbours, and they stood up to them and said, "Why are you taking these young men away? They're not to blame for anything." But the man who had his weapon pointed at me said, "Keep quiet or I'll shoot you, fill you with lead." That's what I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Once you arrived at the Motel Sretno, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: When we arrived -- or rather, when I arrived at the motel, I found about seven or eight other detainees there. That's my estimate, at least. And I, of course, thought that I was going to be questioned, interrogated, and that they would take me into an office somewhere. And I had faith in the fact that I was born in Kakanj, that I went to school there, I graduated from secondary school there and went to school with some people who were in authority now and that some of the professors who were in power used to teach me. So I didn't think that I was to blame for anything, that I would just be questioned and allowed to go home. This did not happen. They took us to the basement of the motel straight away. I think it was part of the boiler room of the motel, in fact. And some five or ten minutes later they started beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were mentioning that at the point in time you arrived at the Motel Sretno there were already seven or eight other detainees there. These detainees, were they all men or were there also women amongst them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: They were all men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber about the ethnicity of these men, as far as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: At the end, when all the detainees were brought in - and there were 16 of us - I know exactly who was who. Of the 16, there were 12 Croats and 4 of the Orthodox faith, or Serbs, whichever you like to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These 16 Croats and Serbs, were they civilians or were they members of any army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, of those 16 of us who were detained, all of us were civilians except for one man, who was wearing a uniform. The bottom part was a camouflage uniform. And I know his name was Lovro, his first name. I don't know his surname. He was a refugee in Kakanj. And I think that he was the only one who was a member of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please provide the Trial Chamber with the names of the other detainees as far as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I know quite a lot of them, their names, because they were all neighbours of mine. There was myself, Marinko Marusic; and my brother, Josip; Petrovic Nikola, who's already been here in the courtroom; then there was Zeljko Krkeljas and his brother, Mladenko Krkeljas; then there was Radovan Blazenovic and another young man from Catici, Nenad Bogelja. And there were some refugees who were from Ilijas. And we were all put up there. I just know their first names. There was a man called Drago. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At what point in time during the 18th of May, 1993 were you the 16 detainees you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the group increased in number until there were finally 16 of us. Nikola Petrovic was brought in after me, and he's just testified. Then Nenad Bogelja was brought in, and some others. I can't remember exactly, but after an hour or an hour and a half, there were a total of 16 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These 16 detainees, were they all put in the very same room?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe the size of this room.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the room was one space, but on the left-hand side there were some iron bars, and we were in that part behind the bars. And that part might have been about 30 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What about the light in this detention room?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: There was no light in the room. It was a damp room, and the floor was concrete. And it was wet too, fairly dirty as well, and it was a rough surface. It wasn't a smooth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what happened to you after you had been brought to this detention room.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, I was brought into the room, and I thought we would be going somewhere else, leaving the room. But about five or ten minutes later they took me out, and without any warning at all or without asking me anything they began beating me. I just tried to ask them why they were beating us and why have you arrested us. Because I said I felt myself to be a Bosnian, and that's why I stayed at home. However, one of the men, one of the members of the unit, swore at me and said that they were creating a dzamahirija and that there was no Bosnia. And then they started beating me. And after that, every conversation ended in my being beaten even more. And the other men told me that the same thing happened to them. So that by the end of the day we just decided to keep quiet and just take the beatings in silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, Mr. Marusic, what does a dzamahirija, what does it actually mean?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact translation, but I think that this member of the unit who beat me meant that he belonged to a unit which was established -- in the process of establishing a Muslim state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what objects have been used to beat you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: They beat us with a variety of objects. There were the wooden batons and rifle butts. They also beat me with a metal hook. It was in the shape of an "S." And they beat us on the shoulders, mostly, with that metal hook. Then they would beat us with the back of a metal chair. It was -- the back was made up of a metal rod. And they were wearing boots, so they kicked us with their boots and their fists, and they even beat us with a chain. But it was difficult for them to wield the chain, so that they decided to leave the chain and use the other implements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The ones who beat you, were these civilians or were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you see any military insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I noticed that they were wearing uniforms, military uniforms. And on their belts they had the MOS emblem that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it the very same emblem as you described earlier on in respect to the soldier who actually arrested you the very same day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I forgot to say a moment ago that all of them had long beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These soldiers with the long beards, were they local soldiers or were they foreign soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they were local ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How often have you been beaten in the course of this night?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was beaten four times, and they would take us out one by one so that all of us were beaten in the same way mostly and as much as each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At what part of your body have you been beaten?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: They beat us all over our bodies. And I assume that they were people who knew some combat skills already, because they knew exactly at which points to beat us. They beat me in the region of my liver and my genitalia and on my back and head.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: The area of my heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did they also beat you on your head?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were there any --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we have a mistake in the interpretation. Line 10 says that he was beaten in the region of his liver, back, head, but there's also the word "genitalia." And the witness did not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as line 10 is concerned, we can ask the question again so that he can say exactly where he was beaten on his body, if there was a query there. So, Mr. Withopf, would you ask the witness to be specific and tell us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, you were describing that you have been beaten in the region of your liver, in the region of your back, in the area of your heart, and in the area of your head. Have there been any other body parts you have been beaten at?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The worst injuries were around my liver and also on my back, and I have haematoma from the beatings. As for the other detainees, on the photographs I saw later on, I saw that there were considerable injuries to the arms and legs which were caused when they tried to protect themselves from the blows, to protect their arms and legs from the blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall any other beatings, beatings that haven't been inflicted by the guards on you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you been ordered -- have the detainees been ordered to beat each other?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat me a total of four times, as I have already said. And they forced me to beat the witness that was here a moment ago, Nikola Petrovic, and they did that on two occasions. The first time we had to beat each other with our fists. And when they thought that we weren't beating each other strongly enough, that the blows weren't hard enough, instead of me, they would step in and start beating us, either him or me, so that the two of us had to slap each other and hit each other. That was the first time. The second time, they ordered me -- they ordered Nikola to lie down and ordered me to kick him in the kidney region. I tried to make -- to avoid kicking him in the ribs and kidneys, and I would kick him a little lower down in the hip area. But they didn't like that, so then I had to lie down and one of the soldiers jumped on me. I was lying down on my stomach. He jumped on my chest and hit me a couple of times, kicked me with his legs, and then said, "See, that's how it's done." And then he hit Nikola himself several times, instead of hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of this night, have you been ordered by the ones who beat you to shout something?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to shout words like "Allah-U-Ekber" and when they said "Tekbir." So they would say "Tekbir," and our response would have to be "Allah-U-Ekber." And we had to repeat that as much as 100 times perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to whether all 16 detainees have been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of us were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to whether all 16 detainees have been beaten to the very same extent as you have been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: We were mostly beaten -- all of us were beaten, mostly, I think, to the same degree; the same extent, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Marusic, about the injuries which have been the result of these beatings, about your injuries.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: My injuries -- well, when I was dragged home - I wasn't able to go home on my own - my back was all black and blue. You couldn't put your finger anywhere in a spot that wasn't black or blue, bruised. I was in a semiconscious state, and I couldn't see properly. My eyes were glazed over. The initial findings, when I was examined, showed that my liver had been enlarged, that I had a haematoma underneath my left and right ribcage, that my sedimentation was high. So that's as far as I'm concerned. I also had an injury on the left side of my head here. That's as far as my injuries go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What do you know about the injuries of the other detainees as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know about the injuries of the people I met shortly after that event. Mr. Nikola Petrovic had also sustained grave injuries; that's the young man who preceded me. He had injuries to the head. I think he had seven stitches. Because of that wound, he still has to see a neuropsychiatrist even today. I don't think his situation is a good one, as far as that is concerned. And that concerns that wound. He also had wounds to the back. The backs of all of us had been bruised, and our arms as well. And there were quite a few injuries to the legs. My brother's bone was fissured. It was either the left or the right arm - I think it was the left - and it was in plaster. I know about Bogelja Nenad, that he had also sustained quite serious injuries. I think they asked him to bring them some kind of money. He said he should -- he would go and get all the money so long as they didn't beat him up. He said he had two children. But that didn't help him at all. So all the injuries were quite serious ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, do you still suffer today from the injuries that have been the result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I still have trouble, problems because of the consequences. I have problems with my liver, which shows up in the findings. I still have high sedimentation. And I haven't checked this, but I have certain psychological problems. A sad film can make me cry very easily, or when I see what the fate of some children is, this affects me. I'm quite sensitive when it comes to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At what point in time during the night from the 18th to the 19th of May, 1993, did the beatings stop?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: The beatings stopped sometime in the morning, at 4.00 in the morning. And if I hadn't been -- if we hadn't been saved by someone, I don't think the beatings would have stopped. The guard who was guarding us, he ran out of cigarettes and he went to get some cigarettes and he locked the bars behind which we were located so that sometime around 4.00 in the morning these young men turned up as usual, probably to beat us again, but on that occasion I saw that they had knives on them too. But they weren't able to enter, since the chain had been locked. They asked us where the guard was. And out of fear, we said that he'd gone to get some cigarettes. I think that this is what saved us, because I for sure, and probably four or five other young men, would certainly not have been able to withstand another beating.
