utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you have been questioned at the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the longest night. We could hardly wait for a new day. At around 6.00 in the morning they interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The ones who interrogated you, were they the same individuals as the ones who beat you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated by a gentleman in civilian clothing. He wasn't in uniform. I don't know what his name was. He was dark, heavy built, fairly good-looking, and a member of the MOS was standing by his side. He had a beard, and that MOS member who appeared in the morning is someone I knew. At the time, I did not recognise him. I know his first and last name. We worked together in Travnik. And that young man, that member, as I was his boss, he helped me wash in the morning -- or rather, he washed me, and he offered to take me home. And it wasn't until we got into the car -- I didn't recognise him. He said who he was. He said, "You know that I worked with you," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How did you know that this person who was standing beside the person in civilian clothing has been a MOS member at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the uniform he was in. He had a long beard -- he had a long beard, and he had a belt which identified him. It was quite clear from the belt that the unit concerned belonged to the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there anybody else other than the man in civilian clothing, the other man in a MOS uniform, was there anybody else who was present during the questioning?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Not when they interrogated me, not at that time. There were only the two of them. But in the morning, when they lined us up, when we were released, I don't remember there being anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did they question you about?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the member I've mentioned, the one who took me home, the one I had worked with, he was standing on the side in an upright position. He didn't say anything. Only the gentleman who was sitting there and kept a record, it was only he who asked us for our names, places of birth, where we were employed, what sort of units we had been members of, what our jobs in Kakanj were at the time. He asked us such questions, questions of a general nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time on this day when you actually have been released?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was perhaps the first one to be released, since this young man knew me. He helped me and my brother. I told him that my brother was detained there too. He said when we were alone that he -- that if he had known that I was there, nothing would have happened to me, most likely. I said that all the others were just as guilty as I was; in other words, that no one was guilty, because all the people there were civilians. I asked him if he could help my brother too, because I was feeling sure of myself to a certain extent. He asked me who my brother was, and I said that it was the young man in the chequered shirt. And he said, "Tell him to go out now so that I know who he is." And in the morning, when they interrogated us, he helped me wash. He took me out of the motel. I was released perhaps -- well, I can't say exactly now, but I think it was about 8.00 in the morning, and MOS members were sitting around the motel near the parking on the grass, and they insulted me because of my ethnic membership and they also shouted out "Allah-U-Ekber" to me. He told me to remain silent. He said I shouldn't react. He took me as far as the car. I think it was a jeep. And he took me to my house. Naturally, I thanked him and asked him if he wanted to come in with me. He said that he was ashamed and that there was no sense in him entering my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you have been -- you have been questioned, were your injuries still visible?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know whether the other detainees were questioned as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't aware of what was happening in the military sense in Kakanj. They interrogated me. They interrogated my brother. I don't know how many others were interrogated. But all I know is that all the Croats were released that morning and earlier than the Serbs, before the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, in the course of today's testimony, you a number of times referred to Niko Petrovic who you identified as having testified earlier on today. Did you recently talk to Mr. Niko Petrovic in respect to your testimony here before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: To Niko? Well, no, not until I, too, was called to testify. We are quite different characters. I think that this testimony unsettled him quite a lot. I think that he even complained to me about not being able to sleep when he received the summons to come and testify. But until the last moment I didn't even tell him that I was going to testify for that very reason, because there's nothing more to be said. I mean, you can say a lot of things, but you end up not saying anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Marusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before the Defence takes the floor for its cross-examination, I would like you to tell me who the person who released you and took you to your home was. You invited him in, but the person refused to go into your house. Who was this person, someone you must have known?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Ismet Dervic. He worked in the furniture factory in the place called Turbe, near Travnik. I was his boss. He worked for me on a lathe. He was a good worker. I know that he trained karate. At the time I think that he had a black belt. And he lives in Travnik in the village of Bijelo Buce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as he was in the detention facility, what was his position? Was he a civilian? Was he a member of the military? As far as you know, what duties did he perform?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in uniform, so he was a member of the military. But I don't know exactly what duties he performed, but I assume that he may have been the bodyguard of the person who interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to the best of your knowledge, did he hold a superior position or a subordinate position?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I think he was a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now ask the Defence to proceed with their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Marusic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Hadzihasanovic. And I would appreciate it if you could answer a number of questions of mine.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you went to Kakanj again in 1992 and that you believed that it was a safer place for you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Kakanj and before the events that you have described to the Trial Chamber today, you were not a member of a military formation of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you were aware of the fact that there were BH Army units in Kakanj, as well as units of the HVO; there were HVO brigades there.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until April 1993, the HVO brigade was deployed in the centre of Kakanj in the so-called Elementara and it then relocated to the village of Haljinici 5 kilometres east of the city towards Vares and Kraljeva Sutjeska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993, you were able to follow the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed or you found out that although it was fairly peaceful in Kakanj, an armed conflict between the BH Army and the HVO had broken out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, these conflicts were ongoing in the area of Kiseljak and Busovaca, and in April they were ongoing in Vitez, Ahmici, and in other parts of Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This realisation also made the fear of uncontrolled revenge taken by individuals against the inhabitants of other nationalities in Kakanj itself. It made this fear even greater. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before these events and because of this tension, some of the Croats started leaving Kakanj, but you and your family didn't leave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, the HVO issued appeals to the Croatian population to withdraw in the direction of Vares and Busovaca, but as you said, you felt that you were a Bosnian and you thought that you should remain at home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to point out that no one asked me to withdraw, as I wasn't a member of a unit of any kind. Because of my personal feelings, I remained at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you know that some people did receive such appeals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about anyone receiving appeals. Perhaps. But I really didn't receive anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you said, on the 18th of May, at around 1700 hours a number of soldiers came to collect you and they came to your house and they took you to the Sretno Motel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could see that those soldiers were fairly frustrated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the word "frustrated" means. Perhaps I'd use a different and more appropriate word. I don't think it was a matter of frustration. To me they seemed, well, I would say drugged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you testified about your maltreatment in the basement of the Sretno Motel. You said that one of them said that this would be a dzamahirija.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this hearing, you told an investigator from The Hague -- you gave an investigator from The Hague Tribunal a statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't mention what this soldier told you to this person, to the investigator, because it didn't come to mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I testified with regard to that earlier on, but what I have claimed about what this person told me is correct. But there are many other details that I have not testified about today either. I thought that this was quite sufficient. But the claim I made, that this is what I was told when I asked a question, is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One of those soldiers also told you, you thought that no revenge would be taken because of Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you knew that a month before you had been taken away there was a massacre in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was a massacre against the Muslim population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At about 4.00 in the morning on the following day, on the 19th of May, you said that you were detained or, rather, locked up in this part of the basement, and that saved all of you from additional maltreatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So after this soldier who had locked you up went to get cigarettes, after that, none of you suffered further maltreatment at the hands of the soldiers who had maltreated you in the course of the night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people who interrogated you early in the morning - and you said that one of them was a civilian - you said that one of them was called Ismet Dervic - these persons weren't in the basement at night. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of that interrogation, you weren't maltreated at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that interrogation -- or rather, shortly after the interrogation had been concluded, this soldier took you to your house. He drove you there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: After that, did you remain in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Mr. Kubura's Defence team have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If the Prosecution doesn't have any further questions -- I'll turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you for having come to The Hague to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence. You've answered all the questions put to you. We thank you for your testimony, and we wish you a good trip home. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no further questions or comments to be made by either of the sides, we will resume tomorrow at 9.00, since we will be sitting in the morning this week, unless Mr. Withopf has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution wishes to address a number of issues related to the witness schedule for this week. Since such issues also relate to applications for protective measures, I would like to address these issues in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.25 p.m.,
